title_topic: Ceilings of care and treatment escalation plans
summary: A consultant-level, legally precise review of ceilings of care. Evidence: the Cambridge UFTO before-and-after study (PLoS One 2013) found fewer harms in patients not for CPR (rate difference 12.9 per 1000 patient-days; harms contributing to death 23/71 vs 4/44); a 2025 randomised vignette study showed a DNACPR decision reduced geriatricians' willingness to consider NIV (67.3% vs 83.6%) and ICU (10.9% vs 25.5%); the NIHR ReSPECT evaluation (2022) found ReSPECT in 40 of 186 acute hospitals by late 2019, patient/family involvement recorded on 73% of forms, similar harms with or without a form, and conversations ranging from open to 'informing of a decision already made'; a Leeds analysis of 23,729 ReSPECT plans found DNACPR less often recorded for Asian and Black than White patients. Law: Burke [2005] EWCA Civ 1003 (no obligation to provide treatment not clinically indicated, paras 50 and 55, but para 53 on competent patients wanting ANH); Aintree v James [2013] UKSC 67 (court has no greater power than patient, para 18; question is whether giving treatment is in best interests, para 22; widest-sense welfare and consultation, para 39; patient's own perspective, para 45; advance applications, para 47); N v ACCG [2017] UKSC 22 (choice only between available options, para 35); Tracey [2014] EWCA Civ 822 (Article 8 presumption of patient involvement in DNACPR, paras 53 to 55; common law the same, para 89); Winspear [2015] EWHC 3250 (QB) (s4(7) MCA duty to consult carer, paras 45, 50, 52, 59). The pivotal 2026 development is Townsend v Epsom and St Helier [2026] EWCA Civ 195: no carve-out for 'clinical decisions' in incapacitated adults (para 69); unresolved disagreement about life-sustaining treatment must go to court via the commissioner and the hospital cannot pre-empt it by unilateral withholding or withdrawal (para 72); but the court can never compel treatment clinicians consider clinically inappropriate (paras 68(5), 74). The Supreme Court granted permission on 29 June 2026 with the hearing listed for 12 to 13 January 2027. Royal Free v RH [2026] EWCOP 17 (T3) shows trusts starting treatment pending court resolution after Townsend, and a court-approved, permissive ceiling of care. GMC end-of-life guidance (2010, updated 2022 and 2024) paras 16, 47 to 48, 134, 138, 143; joint BMA/RCUK/RCN CPR guidance (3rd edition, 1st revision 2016) is under review; the MCA Code of Practice has not been revised since 2007. Communication advice separates what medicine can achieve from what the patient would want, and avoids asking families to decide (GSTT v VA [2023] EWCOP 39, para 20).
takeaways: A ceiling of care for an incapacitated patient is a best interests decision under the Mental Capacity Act: after Townsend [2026] EWCA Civ 195 (para 69) there is no carve-out for 'clinical decisions'.

Nobody, including the Court of Protection, can compel you to give treatment you consider clinically inappropriate (Burke paras 50 and 55; Aintree para 18; N v ACCG para 35; Townsend paras 68(5) and 74).

Consult before you record a DNACPR decision: the patient unless it is likely to cause harm (Tracey paras 53 to 55), and the family or carer of an incapacitated patient unless impracticable (Winspear, s4(7) MCA); record why if you do not.
Use a TEP or ReSPECT plan to place DNACPR within a wider plan (it applies only to CPR, GMC para 143), and share second opinions with the family promptly.

Unresolved disagreement about life-sustaining treatment should go to court via the commissioning body, early (Townsend para 72; Re Y para 125); watch for the Supreme Court hearing on 12 to 13 January 2027.
